content.text: A leaderboard score tells you how a model did on someone else's questions, graded someone else's way, and some models have already seen those questions or were tuned for that leaderboard. Use public scores to build a shortlist, then pick with your own eval: your inputs, your success criteria, and the cost and latency you can afford.

A team needs a model to summarize support tickets in English and Egyptian Arabic. They pick the one at the top of a popular leaderboard, with the best reasoning and math scores of the month. In production, English summaries are fine, but Arabic tickets lose their order numbers, responses take twice the latency budget, and the bill is the largest line in the project. Weeks later, someone runs a cheaper model on fifty real tickets. It does as well. The leaderboard had answered a different question from theirs.
The common misconception
"The model with the highest public benchmark score will be the best one for my use case." It's an easy rule to follow:

items.text: A number looks objective, and the benchmarks are large, standardized and public.
Model launches lead with benchmark tables, so the industry seems to agree that they decide.
Reading a ranking takes a minute; building an eval takes days.
Scores do track general capability: a model at the top is rarely weak.

content.text: The half-truth: benchmarks are useful evidence of broad capability, and a fine way to build a shortlist. But a score answers "how did this model do on these questions, scored this way?" Several things separate that answer from yours.
What actually happens
The test may be in the training data
Models train on huge scrapes of the web, and public benchmarks are on the web. When test examples end up in the training data, that's
data contamination
, and the score measures memory as well as skill.

Golchin and Surdeanu showed in 2023 how to detect it from the outside. Their "guided instruction" gives the model the dataset's name, the partition and the start of a test example, and asks it to finish. If it reproduces the rest exactly or nearly, the example was likely seen. Their best method agreed with human experts 92% to 100% of the time across seven datasets, and it found GPT-4 contaminated with AG News, WNLI and XSum.

Deng and colleagues tried a sharper probe the same year: hide one wrong option in a multiple-choice question and ask the model to fill it in. A wrong option is arbitrary, so it's hard to guess from the question alone. On MMLU, ChatGPT and GPT-4 reproduced the missing option exactly 52% and 57% of the time.
Fresh questions expose overfitting

If a score reflects skill, a new test of the same difficulty should give the same score. Zhang and colleagues at Scale AI built that test in 2024: GSM1k, 1,205 new grade-school math problems written to mirror the popular GSM8k benchmark. Some models dropped by up to 8% in accuracy. Several families, including Phi and Mistral, showed systematic overfitting across almost all their sizes, while frontier models such as GPT, Gemini and Claude showed minimal signs of it, and all models broadly solved new problems. The lesson isn't that benchmarks lie. It's that they can overstate, by different amounts for different models, so a gap of a few points may not be a gap in skill.
Leaderboards can be optimized for

Rankings based on human votes have their own distortions. In The Leaderboard Illusion, Singh and colleagues studied Chatbot Arena in 2025. They found that a handful of providers privately tested many variants before release and could publish only the best score; at the extreme, Meta tested 27 private variants before the Llama 4 release. They also estimated that access to Arena data could raise performance on the Arena's own distribution by up to 112% in relative terms. Their conclusion: these dynamics reward overfitting to the Arena, not general model quality.
Your task isn't the benchmark

Even a perfectly clean benchmark measures its prompts, its languages, its output format and its grader. Your feature has its own: real tickets, two languages, a summary that must keep the order number, a latency budget and a price. Anthropic's model guide puts it directly: create tests specific to your use case, since a good evaluation set is the most important step in choosing a model. Test with your actual prompts and data, compare accuracy, quality and edge cases, and weigh performance against cost. The guide also notes that tuning a model's effort setting is often a better lever than switching models.
Choosing by leaderboard, choosing by eval
The first version ships whatever tops the leaderboard. The second runs each candidate on your own labeled tickets and reports pass rate, cost and latency side by side.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Ship whichever model tops this week's public leaderboard
scores = load_leaderboard("reasoning")  # someone else's questions
MODEL = max(scores, key=scores.get)
# Never run on a real ticket, in Arabic or within your latency budget

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import time
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
CANDIDATES = ["claude-opus-5-5", "claude-sonnet-5-5", "claude-haiku-5-5"]

for model in CANDIDATES:
    passed, cost, start = 0, 0.0, time.perf_counter()
    for case in CASES:  # real tickets in both languages, labeled by support
        reply = client.messages.create(
            model=model, max_tokens=16000, system=SUMMARY_PROMPT,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case["ticket"]}],
        )
        text = next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")
        passed += grade(text, case["must_mention"])  # your criteria
        cost += price(model, reply.usage)  # from the token counts
    secs = (time.perf_counter() - start) / len(CASES)
    print(f"{model}: {passed / len(CASES):.0%} passed, "
          f"${cost:.2f}, {secs:.1f}s per ticket")

content.text: The eval answers the team's actual question: which model keeps the order number in Arabic and English, at what price and speed. The earlier article on
evals
in this path covers building the cases and the grader; here they decide the model.

content.text: Keep part of your eval cases out of prompt tuning and never paste them into public tools. Refresh them with new production cases now and then. That's how you stop your own eval from turning into a benchmark your prompts have memorized.

blocks.title: A few points is often noise

content.text: Differences of a few points can come from contamination or selective reporting rather than skill, as GSM1k and the Arena study showed. Your own eval has noise too: on 50 cases, a single case is 2 percentage points. Run several trials, and don't switch models over a gap smaller than what one or two cases can produce.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Shortlist with benchmarks, don't choose with them

content.text: Use public scores to pick two to four candidates, favoring benchmarks close to your task and results on newly written questions.

items.title: Build the eval from real traffic

content.text: Collect real inputs in every language and format you serve, with written success criteria and a grader.

items.title: Run every candidate on the same cases

content.text: Record pass rate, cost and latency per case, with several trials per case, and read the failures.
Try prompt changes and effort settings on the current model before paying for a bigger one.
When a new model or version ships, run it on your eval before believing its launch table.
Key takeaways

items.text: A benchmark score measures one set of questions graded one way, not your feature.
Contamination is real: models have reproduced hidden test content, and some dropped by up to 8% on fresh lookalike questions.
Leaderboards can reward selective testing and tuning for the leaderboard itself.
Pick models with your own eval: your inputs, criteria, cost and latency.
Use benchmarks for a shortlist, and keep part of your own eval private and fresh.
